questions.prompt: Which exercise types does he list as core musicianship practice?
choices: A Only orchestration for full symphony.
B Rhythmic dictation, melodic dictation, harmonic dictation, and rhythmic clapback.
C Exclusive use of DAW grid quantization.
D Only memorizing composer birth years.
questions.explain: Those four exercise families cover flexible musicianship skills he emphasizes.

questions.prompt: Why does he urge singing back a melody before writing melodic dictation?
choices: A Singing is forbidden in ear training.
B If you can sing it, you are likelier to retain it and write it accurately; audition/inner hearing precedes reproduction.
C Singing replaces the need for any notation.
D Only instrumentalists need inner hearing.
questions.explain: Singing back aids retention and writing; earlier he stresses audiation before playing (7.25).

questions.prompt: What mnemonic does he offer for the hard-to-sing tritone?
choices: A The opening of Beethoven’s Fifth exclusively.
B The first two notes of The Simpsons theme.
C Only solfège syllable “do–do”.
D Counting ledger lines aloud.
questions.explain: Tritone (three whole tones) is hard to sing; he uses The Simpsons theme as a mnemonic.

questions.prompt: How does he distinguish hearing from listening?
choices: A They are identical physiological events.
B Hearing is indifferent physiology (airwaves on the eardrum); listening requires culture, intention, and understanding.
C Listening is only about volume levels.
D Hearing requires years of theory study; listening does not.
questions.explain: Hearing = physical; listening = cultivated, intentional understanding.

questions.prompt: Before clapback in 6/8, what pulse grouping should be in your ear?
choices: A Six equal strong beats with no grouping.
B Two pulse groups of three eighths each (compound duple feel).
C Only a single undivided whole-note pulse.
D Strict 4/4 accents on every sixteenth.
questions.explain: 6/8 has six eighths but is articulated as two groups of three—feel that before clapback.
